source: Lee, Oh, Kim, Shin, Tack (2025) ReVISE: Learning to Refine at Test-Time via Intrinsic Self-Verification (ICML 2025)
finding: Core design. After the first answer the model emits one special token: [eos] (stop) or [refine] (rewrite). Two-stage curriculum using DPO plus SFT loss. Stage 1 teaches the verify token from the model's own correct and wrong samples. Stage 2 teaches correction by pairing a wrong attempt with the gold answer.
numbers: Stage 1 pairs: correct answer -> prefer [eos] over [refine]; wrong answer -> prefer [refine] over [eos]. Stage 2 starts from the stage 1 model. Loss = SFT + beta*DPO. One reasoning path sampled per training item (about 50,000 generations in the SCoRe comparison).
quote: ReVISE first learns to check correctness, then learns to improve wrong reasoning
limits: Needs ground-truth labels for the training questions. Tested only on Llama-3.2-1B, Llama-3.1-8B (plus Gemma-2-2B in appendix); math and one code set. Refine step is trained on the gold answer, not on the model's own successful repairs.
agent_relevance: This is the learned version of our S5 trigger: a cheap stop-or-refine signal read from the model itself after attempt one, then a revision only on [refine]. The trigger is a probability we can read in code (G5), not a prose self-judgement.

source: Lee, Oh, Kim, Shin, Tack (2025) ReVISE: Learning to Refine at Test-Time via Intrinsic Self-Verification (ICML 2025) - main results (Table 1)
finding: ReVISE beats few-shot CoT, SFT, RFT and STaR+ on first-attempt accuracy and with five-sample voting that uses its own verify probability as the vote weight.
limits: Gains over the strongest baseline at Maj@1 are small (about 1 to 3 points). The bigger Maj@5 gain mixes two effects: ReVISE uses confidence weights, baselines use plain votes. No error bars in Table 1. Base models are weak (1B, 8B).
agent_relevance: A learned trigger gives a modest first-attempt lift; most extra gain comes from using the verify probability as a vote weight. Fits G5: code does the weighting.

source: Lee, Oh, Kim, Shin, Tack (2025) ReVISE: Learning to Refine at Test-Time via Intrinsic Self-Verification (ICML 2025) - headline Maj@3 numbers (intro)
finding: Authors report that confidence-aware voting with three samples lifts accuracy from 27.1 to 31.1 on GSM8K (Llama-3.2-1B) and 33.2 to 36.0 on MATH (Llama-3.1-8B).
limits: Intro numbers. The baseline compared against is not one clean row of Table 1. Treat as headline, not as the strict controlled result.
agent_relevance: Size to expect from a trained trigger on small models: low single digits.

source: Lee, Oh, Kim, Shin, Tack (2025) ReVISE: Learning to Refine at Test-Time via Intrinsic Self-Verification (ICML 2025) - curriculum and verification quality (Fig 3, Fig 4)
finding: Two-stage curriculum beats training both tasks at once on the same preference data. Verification quality (AUROC of the [eos] probability against true correctness) rises with the curriculum, but stage 2 slightly hurts verification (forgetting).
numbers: Llama-3.2-1B GSM8K: no curriculum 22.6% -> curriculum 28.1% accuracy; verify AUROC 71% -> 76%. Without DPO (SFT only): 10.3 points lower accuracy.
limits: Single small model and dataset for the ablation. AUROC 76% is far from reliable.
agent_relevance: A learned trigger reaches only about 0.76 AUROC even after targeted training. Our S5 trigger should not trust one self-confidence number; pair it with a code check (G2, G3).

source: Lee, Oh, Kim, Shin, Tack (2025) ReVISE: Learning to Refine at Test-Time via Intrinsic Self-Verification (ICML 2025) - does it truly refine? (First vs Retry, Fig 7) and confidence histogram (Fig 5)
finding: ReVISE beats two controls: First (stop at the refine token, keep the first answer) and Retry (draw a fresh sample when the model says refine). So the gain is from real refinement, not just resampling. Correct answers show higher [eos] probability than wrong ones; the decision threshold is M([eos]) - M([refine]) = 0.
numbers: Bar values only in a figure, not extractable here. Retry uses temperature 0.7 for the second sample; First and ReVISE decode greedily.
limits: Greedy vs sampled is not exactly equal compute. Figure values not read as numbers.
agent_relevance: The right control for any refine trigger is resample-on-trigger. Our schema should run that control (G7).

source: Lee, Oh, Kim, Shin, Tack (2025) ReVISE: Learning to Refine at Test-Time via Intrinsic Self-Verification (ICML 2025) - instruct model and domain transfer (Tables 3, 4)
finding: On an already instruction-tuned model, ordinary SFT and RFT fine-tuning hurt, but ReVISE helps. Trained on MATH and tested on GSM8K, ReVISE keeps a small edge.
numbers: Llama-3.2-1B-Instruct GSM8K: zero-shot CoT 48.6; SFT 41.9; RFT 44.0; ReVISE 52.3 (with the larger GSM240K data: 48.6 / 54.8 / 50.9 / 59.4). Transfer MATH->GSM8K: 1B SFT 7.3, RFT 8.2, STaR+ 8.0, ReVISE 8.8; 8B SFT 60.3, RFT 60.3, STaR+ 58.7, ReVISE 61.5.
limits: Transfer edge is 0.6 to 1.2 points, plausibly noise (no CIs). Instruct result is on one 1B model.
agent_relevance: The edge from a learned trigger survives a domain shift only barely. Do not expect transfer to our tasks without testing.

source: Lee, Oh, Kim, Shin, Tack (2025) ReVISE: Learning to Refine at Test-Time via Intrinsic Self-Verification (ICML 2025) - vs SCoRe, V-STaR verifier, scaling, iteration (App. B)
finding: Against Google's RL method SCoRe on Gemma-2-2B MATH-500, ReVISE matches or beats it at about 1/30 of the generations. Its built-in verifier beats a separately trained V-STaR verifier in AUROC. Accuracy keeps rising with up to 3 refine rounds and with more voting samples.
numbers: MATH-500 Gemma-2-2B: CoT 16.8; SFT 17.6; RFT 18.6; SCoRe 23.0; ReVISE 23.2 (30x cheaper); +iter1 24.2; +iter2 25.8. GSM8K AUROC: V-STaR verifier 69.5 vs ReVISE 76.0. GSM8K Llama-3.2-1B ReVISE Maj@2 to Maj@64: 28.3 up to 37.7 (Maj@64 37.7).
limits: SCoRe number copied from its paper (no open code). The PDF text extraction shuffled the baseline row labels in the Maj@K table, so only the ReVISE row is quoted.
agent_relevance: Evidence that a trained self-verifier at small scale can rival a separate verifier; supports a one-model trigger, at the cost of a training run.

source: Huang, Chen, Mishra, Zheng, Yu, Song, Zhou (2024) Large Language Models Cannot Self-Correct Reasoning Yet (ICLR 2024)
finding: Founding negative result. With no outside signal (intrinsic self-correction), asking GPT-3.5, GPT-4, GPT-4-Turbo and Llama-2 to review and fix their reasoning lowers accuracy. Earlier positive results used the gold label to decide when to stop.
quote: LLMs struggle to self-correct their responses without external feedback, and at times, their performance even degrades
limits: Prompted only, no training; 2023-era models. A trained trigger (ReVISE, SCoRe) is the direct answer to this result.
agent_relevance: This is why G1 and G2 exist: do not refine without a signal.

source: Huang, Chen, Mishra, Zheng, Yu, Song, Zhou (2024) Large Language Models Cannot Self-Correct Reasoning Yet (ICLR 2024) - oracle label and why accuracy drops
finding: With the gold label used to stop the loop, self-correction looks great, but that is an oracle result. Without it, most answers stay the same, and changes go more often from correct to wrong than wrong to correct: the model cannot judge its own reasoning.
numbers: Oracle HotpotQA: GPT-3.5 26.0 -> 49.0; GPT-4 29.0 -> 59.0 (read with confidence). Other oracle cells are in a garbled table and are described only as large gains. GPT-3.5 keeps its first GSM8K answer 74.7% of the time over two rounds.
limits: Table layout in the text extraction is garbled, so only the HotpotQA oracle numbers are quoted.
agent_relevance: Any gain we report must be shown without gold labels in the loop (G3).

source: Huang, Chen, Mishra, Zheng, Yu, Song, Zhou (2024) Large Language Models Cannot Self-Correct Reasoning Yet (ICLR 2024) - multi-agent debate vs self-consistency
finding: Re-ran Du et al.'s multi-agent debate on the full GSM8K test set with gpt-3.5-turbo-0301. Debate beats a single answer but is about equal to self-consistency at 3 responses and clearly worse at equal responses beyond that.
numbers: Single answer 76.7; self-consistency 3 responses 82.5, 6 responses 85.3, 9 responses 88.2; debate 83.2 (3 responses) and 83.0 (9 responses). Constrained generation (CommonGen-Hard): own standard prompt 81.8 vs self-correct 75.1.
limits: Cell mapping of the debate rows reconstructed from garbled layout and checked against the paper text (82.5 vs 83.2 at 3 responses). Original debate paper used 100 questions.
agent_relevance: Spend equal tokens on voting before debate. Supports G4 and G7: simple counting is the control.

source: Kumar, Zhuang, Agarwal et al. (2024) Training Language Models to Self-Correct via Reinforcement Learning (SCoRe)
finding: First method to get a clearly positive net change from the model correcting itself with no outside feedback. Plain SFT or STaR on own repair traces fail: the model copies its first answer or edits only when already wrong. SCoRe uses two-turn online RL, a first stage that keeps turn 1 near the base model, and a reward bonus for improving from turn 1 to turn 2.
numbers: Gemini 1.0 Pro, MATH: base 52.6 -> 41.4 (delta -11.2; wrong->right 4.6%, right->wrong 15.8%); Self-Refine 52.8 -> 51.8 (-1.0); STaR 53.6 -> 54.0 (+0.4); Pair-SFT 52.4 -> 54.2 (+1.8); SCoRe 60.0 -> 64.4 (+4.4; wrong->right 5.8%, right->wrong 1.4%). Headline: +15.6 over base delta on MATH.
quote: SCoRe attains the highest self-correction performance
limits: Needs large-scale RL; only 2 turns. Net change is 4.4 points. The +15.6 is relative to a base whose own self-correction is -11.2.
agent_relevance: The right-to-wrong flip rate (15.8% down to 1.4%) is the key quantity. Our S5 trigger should log it directly.

source: Kumar, Zhuang, Agarwal et al. (2024) Training Language Models to Self-Correct via Reinforcement Learning (SCoRe) - code and ablations
finding: On HumanEval SCoRe gives a large turn-2 gain and the best offline-repair score on MBPP-R. Ablation: without multi-turn training the second attempt is worse than the first; both stages and reward shaping matter.
numbers: Gemini 1.5 Flash HumanEval: base t1 53.7, t2 56.7 (+3.0); Self-Refine 53.7 -> 52.5 (-1.2); Pair-SFT 56.1 -> 54.3 (-1.8); SCoRe 52.4 -> 64.6 (+12.2). MBPP-R: base 47.3, Self-Refine 30.7, Pair-SFT 59.8, SCoRe 60.6. MATH ablation delta: single-turn training t1 61.8, t2 59.4 (-2.4); no stage I +2.2; no reward shaping +2.6; STaR instead of REINFORCE +2.2; full +4.4.
limits: One seed; no intervals. Note SCoRe's first-attempt HumanEval score (52.4) is lower than base (53.7).
agent_relevance: Training for first-attempt quality alone can erase second-attempt value: train trigger and repair jointly.

source: Madaan et al. (2023) Self-Refine: Iterative Refinement with Self-Feedback
finding: Prompted loop: generate, give feedback, refine, repeat, using the same model. Big gains on preference-style tasks, near zero on math, because the model rarely flags errors.
numbers: GPT-4 base -> +Self-Refine: Sentiment Reversal 3.8 -> 36.2; Code Readability 15.0 -> 45.0; Code Optimization 92.9 -> 93.1 (one column group). GPT-3.5 Math reasoning 64.1 -> 64.1 (0.0). ChatGPT feedback said 'everything looks good' on 94% of math instances. With an external error flag the math gains were 5+ points. ChatGPT Code Optimization score by iteration: 22.0, 27.0, 27.9, 28.8.
quote: a consistent-looking reasoning chain can deceive LLMs
limits: Preference tasks were scored by GPT-4 as judge (self-preference risk). Table rows in extraction are interleaved, so only unambiguous cells are quoted.
agent_relevance: The 94% 'looks good' figure is the failure of a prose trigger. Tasks where a model grades itself are suspect (G5).

source: Kamoi, Zhang, Zhang, Han, Zhang (2024) When Can LLMs Actually Correct Their Own Mistakes? A Critical Survey of Self-Correction of LLMs
finding: Survey. Verdict: no prior work shows reliable intrinsic self-correction by in-context prompting on general tasks. It works when reliable outside feedback exists, when tasks are easy to verify or decompose, or with large-scale fine-tuning. Many positive papers used unfair setups (oracle labels, weak initial prompts, stronger prompts for the refine step).
numbers: Three research questions: RQ1 intrinsic, RQ2 with external information, RQ3 final output vs other methods. Checklist tables 7 and 8 for future studies.
quote: no prior work shows reliable evidence of successful self-correction with in-context learning
limits: Judgement-based review up to 2024; does not re-run experiments.
agent_relevance: Gives the boundary condition for our trigger: use it only with an outside check or a trained verifier, and compare against the best initial prompt.

source: Tyen, Mansoor, Carbune, Chen, Mak (2024) LLMs cannot find reasoning errors, but can correct them given the error location (Findings ACL 2024)
finding: Splits self-correction into finding the mistake and fixing it. On BIG-Bench Mistake (5 tasks, human step labels) GPT-4 is the best finder and is still weak. Three prompting styles trade recall against false alarms.
numbers: GPT-4 best overall mistake-finding accuracy 52.87 (direct step-level prompting). Per task: 255 wrong-answer plus 45 right-answer traces (300) for the sampled tasks. Accuracy on no-mistake traces falls as more calls are made per trace. A small classifier trained on out-of-domain data beats prompting a large model.
quote: LLMs cannot find reasoning errors, but can correct them given the error location
limits: Traces come from PaLM 2 CoT on simple algorithmic tasks. Only 45 correct traces per task, so correct-trace results are noisy.
agent_relevance: Strong evidence that the bottleneck for a refine trigger is detection, not repair. A cheap trained detector is a viable trigger.

source: Tyen, Mansoor, Carbune, Chen, Mak (2024) LLMs cannot find reasoning errors, but can correct them given the error location (Findings ACL 2024) - backtracking (Table 6) and classifier threshold
finding: Feeding the true mistake step and regenerating from there improves answers much more than it hurts. A random-location control gains less and hurts more. A classifier at about 60 to 70% accuracy is enough for net gain on most tasks.
numbers: Change in accuracy on originally correct traces: 0.00 to -11.43 points with true location (word sorting -11.11); on originally incorrect traces +18.04 to +43.92 (word sorting +23.53). Random location: correct -6.67 to -15.91; incorrect +5.16 to +21.57. Net gain at classifier accuracy about 60 to 70%.
limits: Per-task assignment of table cells scrambled in extraction (only word sorting confirmed from text). Backtracking draws 8 samples at the step and keeps 1.
agent_relevance: Gives a break-even number: about 60 to 70% accurate localisation is enough. Trigger plus step pointer beats trigger alone (G2).

source: Shinn et al. (2023) Reflexion: Language Agents with Verbal Reinforcement Learning
finding: Agent retries after a failure with a written reflection stored in memory. The trigger is an external signal (tests, environment reward). Ablation on the 50 hardest HumanEval Rust items: without self-written tests the agent cannot tell if its code is right and does worse.
numbers: HumanEval pass@1 91% (GPT-4) vs 80% baseline; AlfWorld +22 absolute; HotPotQA +20. Rust-hard ablation (GPT-4): base 60%, no test generation 52%, no self-reflection 60%, full Reflexion 68%.
quote: the agent is unable to determine if the current implementation is correct without unit tests
limits: Trigger comes from tests or environment reward, not model belief. HumanEval is near saturation for GPT-4.
agent_relevance: Reinforces G3: the refine trigger must be a real run; reflect-then-edit without a test adds nothing.

source: Snell, Lee, Xu, Kumar (2024) Scaling LLM Test-Time Compute Optimally can be More Effective than Scaling Model Parameters
finding: A PaLM 2-S revision model was fine-tuned on its own wrong-to-right chains. Left alone it flips about 38% of correct answers to wrong; a verifier or sequential vote picks the best in the chain. Sequential revisions narrowly beat parallel sampling, and the best split between them depends on question difficulty.
numbers: 38% of correct answers converted to incorrect by the naive revision model. Pass@1 improves with each revision step, even beyond the 4 steps trained. Compute-optimal revision/search matches best-of-N with up to 4x less test-time compute.
limits: Capability-specific fine-tuning was needed to induce revision and verification. MATH only.
agent_relevance: The 38% flip rate is what a trigger exists to reduce. Easy questions: sample in parallel; hard: revise in sequence.

source: Cobbe et al. (2021) Training Verifiers to Solve Math Word Problems (GSM8K)
finding: Founding learned-verifier paper. Sample many solutions, score with a trained verifier, pick the top. Verification scales better with data than fine-tuning and gives a boost like a 30x larger model.
numbers: 6B model with verification slightly outperforms a fine-tuned 175B model on full GSM8K (about 30x model-size equivalent). Verifier ranks 100 solutions per problem; generator trained 2 epochs to build data. Token-level verifiers train slower but end better than solution-level.
quote: verification being a simpler task than generation
limits: GPT-3-era models and a separate verifier network, not an intrinsic one.
agent_relevance: Origin of 'checking is easier than generating'; ReVISE moves the verifier into the same weights.

source: Lightman et al. (2023) Let's Verify Step by Step
finding: Step-level human labels (PRM800K) train a reward model that beats outcome-only supervision.
numbers: PRM best-of-1860 solves 78.2% of a MATH test subset; the same table row also lists 72.4 and 69.6 for the comparison methods (outcome reward model and majority vote, order inferred).
limits: Column labels of the 72.4 and 69.6 cells not confirmed. Needs about 800K human step labels.
agent_relevance: Step-level signal localises the mistake (matches Tyen). Supports G2 'cite the failing step'.

source: Weng et al. (2023) Large Language Models are Better Reasoners with Self-Verification
finding: Backward check: use the candidate answer as a condition, ask the model to recover a masked fact from the question, and rank candidates by the match. Reports gains on arithmetic, commonsense and logic sets.
numbers: Abstract and intro read; per-dataset gains not extracted.
limits: Prompting only, 2022-23 models; later work (Huang et al., Tyen) shows prompted self-checks are weak on harder tasks.
agent_relevance: A backward consistency check is a cheap trigger signal that does not ask the model for an opinion.

source: Miao, Teh, Rainforth (2023) SelfCheck: Using LLMs to Zero-Shot Check Their Own Step-by-Step Reasoning
finding: Per-step regenerate-and-compare check, then weighted voting. Improves over plain majority voting on GSM8K, MathQA and MATH, and raises the share of real-correct solutions among those predicted correct.
numbers: Real-correct share among predicted-correct rises from 67.5 to 76.5 (GSM8K), 59.4 to 82.2 (MathQA), 34.6 to 50.8 (MATH). Earlier self-verification baselines predict 'correct' almost always (true and false positive rates about 100% on MATH, 98% on GSM8K).
limits: Run with GPT-3.5; final accuracy gains modest; the check costs several calls per step.
agent_relevance: Warns of trigger collapse: a self-check that always says 'correct' never fires a refine.

source: Zhang et al. (2025) Reasoning Models Know When They're Right: Probing Hidden States for Self-Verification
finding: A small probe on hidden states predicts whether an intermediate answer inside a reasoning trace is right. It is calibrated and can predict correctness before the answer is written. As an early-exit trigger it cuts tokens by up to 24% with no accuracy loss.
numbers: In-distribution: ROC-AUC above 0.7 and ECE below 0.1 for all probes; R1-Distill-Qwen-32B over 0.9 ROC-AUC on AIME. Probes transfer between MATH and GSM8K but not stably from logic to math, and are less calibrated on AIME when trained on easier sets. Up to 24% fewer inference tokens.
limits: Open-weight distilled reasoning models only; needs hidden states, so not available for API models. Out-of-domain transfer unreliable.
agent_relevance: The closest analogue to a learned S5 trigger: a trained readout of 'am I right' that beats the model's own words. Needs weights access.

source: Tsui (2026) Self-Correction Bench: Uncovering and Addressing the Self-Correction Blind Spot in LLMs (COLM 2026)
finding: The same error injected as user-attributed or as model-attributed: models fix the first and miss the second. So the ability exists but is not activated on own output. Cause linked to SFT data lacking error-correction traces. Appending 'Wait' fixes most of it.
numbers: 14 open non-reasoning models: average blind spot 64.5%. Fine-tuning on 5,306 error-correction traces cuts it by 76.0%. Appending 'Wait' cuts it by 89.3% and raises mean accuracy by 156%. Correction markers appear 179.5% more often on external errors (GSM8K-SC) and 73.6% more (PRM800K-SC). Of errors a model leaves in its own output, 4.3 to 10.8% are caught when shown as external.
quote: models correct external errors but fail on identical internal ones
limits: Synthetic injected errors; non-reasoning models; reasoning models show a much smaller blind spot.
agent_relevance: A bias explanation for Huang et al.: models defend their own text. A cheap fix is to present the answer without authorship, as G5 says.

source: Muennighoff et al. (2025) s1: Simple test-time scaling
finding: Budget forcing: suppress the end-of-thinking token and append 'Wait' to make the model re-check, or cut thinking short. s1-32B trained on 1,000 examples improves with more thinking.
numbers: AIME24 50% -> 57% with budget forcing; abstract states gains up to 27% over o1-preview on MATH and AIME24.
limits: Forced 'Wait' is a schedule, not a learned trigger; gains saturate and over-forcing loops. A limited set of benchmarks.
agent_relevance: Contrast with G1: forced doubt helps here, but our own word-puzzle data (92% plain vs 75% forced) says it can hurt. Test per task.

source: S2R authors (2025) S2R: Teaching LLMs to Self-verify and Self-correct via Reinforcement Learning
finding: Trains verify-then-correct behaviour in two stages: a small supervised start with self-verify and self-correct examples, then outcome-level or process-level RL. Large lift on Qwen2.5-Math-7B.
numbers: With 3.1k initialization samples, Qwen2.5-Math-7B goes from 51.0% to 81.6% (abstract), beating models trained on an equal amount of long-CoT distilled data.
limits: Author list not read; cited by title. Abstract and tables skimmed; ablations not extracted.
agent_relevance: A few thousand verify/correct examples can install the habit; a trigger-style hybrid.

source: DeepSeek-AI (2025) DeepSeek-R1: Incentivizing Reasoning Capability in LLMs via Reinforcement Learning
finding: Pure outcome-reward RL (R1-Zero) yields longer reasoning with spontaneous self-checking, shown as an 'aha moment' where the model says 'Wait' and rechecks. A process reward model is discussed among attempts that did not work.
numbers: Aha-moment example in Table 2; PRM discussion in the unsuccessful-attempts section.
limits: Anecdotal trace for the aha moment; later work (Yue et al.) questions whether RL creates new ability.
agent_relevance: Self-checking can emerge from outcome reward alone, so a trigger can be trained on final-answer correctness.

source: Yue et al. (2025) Does Reinforcement Learning Really Incentivize Reasoning Capacity in LLMs Beyond the Base Model?
finding: Counter-evidence: RL-trained models win at pass@1 but base models win at large pass@k. RL narrows the reasoning boundary, and its paths already lie in the base model's distribution. Distillation does add new patterns.
numbers: RLVR models beat base at small k; base models are higher at large k; six RLVR algorithms perform similarly and are far from the base-model upper bound.
limits: Does not test self-verification directly; covers RLVR in math, code and vision.
agent_relevance: A learned refine policy re-weights existing behaviour; do not expect it to add capability.

source: Lin et al. (2024) CriticBench: Benchmarking LLMs for Critique-Correct Reasoning
finding: 15 datasets, 5 reasoning domains, 17 LLMs scored on generating, critiquing and correcting (GQC). Critique and generation ability are linearly related; critique-focused training helps; logic tasks are easier to correct; some weaker models beat stronger ones in self-critique.
numbers: 17 models; 15 datasets; five domains (math, commonsense, symbolic, code, algorithmic). Abstract-level read.
limits: Per-model figures not extracted.
agent_relevance: Supports testing the trigger itself (critique accuracy), not only final accuracy.

source: Gou et al. (2023) CRITIC: LLMs Can Self-Correct with Tool-Interactive Critiquing
finding: Verify the output with outside tools (search engine, code interpreter), then revise. Stresses outside feedback as the driver of improvement.
numbers: Abstract-level read: gains on free-form QA, math program synthesis and toxicity reduction.
limits: Tool access required; abstract only read.
agent_relevance: Matches G2: the revision must cite real output from a tool.

source: Zhang et al. (2024) Generative Verifiers: Reward Modeling as Next-Token Prediction (GenRM)
finding: A verifier trained with next-token loss can write a chain of thought and vote over verification samples. It beats discriminative and LLM-as-judge verifiers for best-of-N.
numbers: Best-of-N: algorithmic tasks 5% -> 45.3%; GSM8K 73% -> 93.4%; MATH easy-to-hard 28% -> 44.6%; MMLU abstract algebra 37.9% -> 53.5%.
limits: Abstract-level read; uses a separate verifier model.
agent_relevance: A verifier that reasons is the stronger option when a separate checker is allowed.
